ch01.note: Linjiang xian (“The Immortal by the River”) is a fixed ci lyric-pattern, whose set metrical form a poet fills with new words. Each of the five parts of this book opens with such a lyric by the author, folded in here as an epigraph at the head of the part’s first chapter. Both the tune-title line and the part-title, “High Ambitions, Admiring Mulan,” turn on the author’s adopted name: Mulan (慕兰) means “admiring [Hua] Mulan,” the legendary woman warrior who took her father’s place in the army (see the note in Chapter 2). The second stanza’s “grand assembly” is a Women’s Day (8 March) gathering of the Northern Expedition years.

ch01.anchor: Tan Sitong and Tang Caichang, who in the last years
ch01.note: Tan Sitong (1865–1898), a reformer from Liuyang and a schoolmate of the author’s father, was one of the “Six Gentlemen” beheaded at Caishikou in Beijing on 28 September 1898 after the failure of the Hundred Days’ Reform; with his fellow townsman Tang Caichang he is remembered as one of the “Two Heroes of Liuyang.” The execution-eve quatrain quoted later in this chapter invokes the Han-dynasty figures Zhang Jian and Du Gen. Corroborated by standard reference works.

The Autumn Harvest Uprising broke out on 9 September 1927 in the Hunan–Jiangxi border area; Wenjiashi, in Liuyang, is where its columns rallied on 19 September—the famous “Wenjiashi turn,” at which Mao Zedong resolved to lead the forces into the countryside rather than assault Changsha. The memoir places the uprising at Wenjiashi; more exactly, Wenjiashi was its rally and turning point. Corroborated with this qualification.

The author’s birth and school name was thus Huang Zhangding (黄彰定), style name Shuyi. She took the name Mulan (慕兰) in 1926 on joining the revolution (Chapter 3), and the name Dinghui (定慧) later, in 1932; in later life, and in this book’s photograph captions, she is generally called Huang Dinghui. On the birth date: the memoir’s own chronology and Chinese biographies give 18 July 1907, while some English sources give 9 July 1906, a discrepancy arising from Chinese age-reckoning. This edition follows the book.

Qiu Jin (1875–1907), a woman revolutionary and feminist who studied in Japan and joined the anti-Qing movement, was executed at Shaoxing on 15 July 1907. The author invokes her repeatedly as a model, and offers her father’s reverence for Qiu Jin as one reason he supported his daughter’s turn to revolution. Corroborated.

ch02.note: Zhu Jianfan (1883–1932), a progressive educator, founded the school that became the Zhounan Girls’ School in Changsha in 1905, selling family property to endow it. Its alumnae include the pioneers of the women’s movement named here—Xiang Jingyu and Cai Chang—as well as Yang Kaihui and the writer Ding Ling. Corroborated.

The name the author adopted, Mulan (慕兰), means literally “admiring Mulan”—an homage to Hua Mulan of the “Ballad of Mulan,” who went to war in her father’s place and served twelve years without her sex being discovered. The pun by which mu (慕, “to admire”) echoes the mu of Hua Mulan (木兰) cannot be reproduced in English. Her birth name was Huang Zhangding (see the note in Chapter 1).
“The Whole River Red” (Man jiang hong) is a celebrated patriotic ci traditionally attributed to the Southern Song general Yue Fei (1103–1142), long a byword for loyal resistance against invaders.

ch03.note: Wan Xiyan (1903–1928), an early Communist and editor-in-chief of the Hankou Republican Daily, became the author’s first husband at Wuhan. Sent afterward to Jiangxi as a provincial Party leader, he was killed there in 1928, in his mid-twenties. Corroborated.

At this point the reissue reproduces a group photograph on which the author, in 1966, inscribed a lyric to the tune Linjiang xian (“The Immortal by the River”): “Forty years ago, this very day—the high tide, joyously met, at Wuhan. How many then were so bold and free? We raised the anti-imperialist banner; talking and laughing, all were heroes. To make a revolution succeed is truly not easy—through hardship and setback, borne with composure! The red flag, fixed forever, streams in the east wind. Keep youth’s vigor ever green; high spirits, in old age firmer still.” An accompanying editorial note records that when she inscribed these lines she was still under political supervision, yet firmly believed herself innocent—a steadfast revolutionary. The photograph and its inscription are given here in a note so as not to break the sentence they interrupt in the source.

The source sentence breaks off here: after “因为我思想” (“because my thinking…”) the clause is left unfinished, and the text passes to the concluding reflection that follows. The account of Qu Qiubai’s persuasion, and the author’s decision to give up the Soviet trip and return to Wuhan, is taken up at the start of Chapter 4. Rendered as it stands, with the break left visible rather than smoothed over.

The “April Twelfth Incident” of 1927: Chiang Kai-shek, having entered Shanghai, turned on his Communist allies, and with the help of the Green Gang disarmed and massacred the worker pickets and Communists, breaking the first Kuomintang–Communist united front. Chiang set up a rival Nationalist government at Nanjing; the Wuhan government, still in alliance with the Communists, expelled him on 17 April. Corroborated.

ch03.anchor: the three towns of Wuchang, Hanyang, and Hankou
ch03.note: The source prints “Wuhan, Hanyang, and Hankou”; since Wuhan is the collective name for the three towns, the first is an evident slip for Wuchang, and the translation renders it so.

ch04.anchor: recovering the British concessions at Hankou and Jiujiang
ch04.note: In the wake of mass agitation at Hankou over the killing of Chinese by British marines, the Wuhan Nationalist government’s foreign minister Eugene Chen (陈友仁) negotiated with the British chargé O’Malley the two “Chen–O’Malley agreements,” signed 19 February 1927 (Hankou) and 20 February 1927 (Jiujiang), by which Britain surrendered both concessions—the first time China recovered a foreign concession by negotiation. Crowds had physically occupied the concessions in early January; the formal accords followed in late February. The substance of the memoir’s account is corroborated, though its “9 February” runs about ten days ahead of the signed agreements.

ch04.anchor: If it profits the country, I will give my life
ch04.note: A famous couplet by the Qing official Lin Zexu (林则徐, 1785–1850)—the commissioner whose destruction of British opium at Canton in 1839 precipitated the First Opium War—written in 1842 on his way into exile: “苟利国家生死以，岂因祸福避趋之” (“If it profits the country, I will give my life; how should I, for fortune or misfortune, flee or seek it?”). Long a byword for selfless public duty.

ch05.anchor: to take no part in the preparations connected with the armed uprising
ch05.note: At this point the source carries one of the source's four editorial endnotes of its own, citing the Huangmei County Gazetteer, p. 215: on 28 July 1927 the Front Committee leading the Nanchang Uprising sent Liu Bocheng, Nie Rongzhen, and the Jiangxi provincial standing-committee members Wan Xiyan and Huang Dao to a secret joint meeting on the armed uprising; by Party decision Chen Tanqiu, Wan Xiyan, and others did not openly take part, but after the insurgent army moved south carried on the underground struggle at Nanchang, Wan Xiyan writing a tract on the conduct of secret work; in February 1928 he left for a special-committee post in southern Jiangxi, was arrested when that organ was broken up, and was killed on 4 April 1928 at Weifuli within the city of Ganzhou. This gazetteer date and place differ from the memoir’s own statement below that he fell in May 1928 assaulting the county town of Wan’an. Modern scholarship (Southeast University’s archives; the martyrs’ registry) supports the gazetteer’s account—arrest and execution at Ganzhou in early April 1928; the memoir’s May/Wan’an version is uncorroborated. Both are left standing here, as in the source.

ch05.anchor: the August Seventh Conference held in Hankou
ch05.note: The emergency conference of the Chinese Communist Party Central of 7 August 1927, held secretly at Hankou, ended Chen Duxiu’s leadership and his “Right-opportunist” line, set the course of armed uprising and agrarian revolution, and was where Mao Zedong offered his dictum that “political power grows out of the barrel of a gun.” Corroborated.

ch05.anchor: the League provincial secretary-general was Rao Shushi
ch05.note: Rao Shushi (饶漱石, 1903–1975), here a Communist Youth League organizer in Jiangxi, later rose to lead the Party’s East China Bureau. In 1954 he and Gao Gang were condemned in the “Gao–Rao anti-Party alliance,” the first great purge of the People’s Republic; he died in prison. The friction the author records here is written with that later history in view. Corroborated.

ch06.anchor: I again ran into Comrade He Chang
ch06.note: He Chang (贺昌, 1906–1935), of Lishi in Shanxi, an early leader of the Communist Youth League and of the Party’s labor and military work, became the author’s second husband. He was killed in 1935 in southern Jiangxi while covering the rearguard after the main Red Army had set out on the Long March. Corroborated.

ch06.anchor: Xiang Zhongfa was nominally the number-one figure
ch06.note: Xiang Zhongfa (向忠发, 1880–1931), a former Wuhan dockers’ leader, was made general secretary of the Party in 1928 as a worker figurehead while Zhou Enlai and others directed the real work, as the author says. Arrested in Shanghai in June 1931, he gave himself up to the Kuomintang and was executed. Corroborated.

Shen Jianlong (沈剑龙) was the son of Shen Dingyi (沈定一, 1883–1928), a landlord-turned-revolutionary and early Communist. When Yang Zhihua left him to marry Qu Qiubai, the three published a joint newspaper notice of the change and remained on good terms—the model of “noble friendship” Zhou Enlai holds up to the author here. Corroborated.

ch07.anchor: the Japanese-owned Naigai Wata No. 13 Mill
ch07.note: Naigai Wata (内外棉, Naigaiwata Kaisha) was the largest Japanese-owned cotton-spinning concern in Shanghai, running many numbered mills. It was the killing of the worker-organizer Gu Zhenghong at a Naigai Wata mill on 15 May 1925 that helped ignite the May Thirtieth Movement, which the author invokes later in this chapter. Corroborated.

ch07.anchor: Comrade Peng Pai too was unfortunately arrested
ch07.note: Peng Pai (彭湃, 1896–1929), a landlord’s son from Haifeng in Guangdong, founded one of China’s first peasant associations and led the Hailufeng peasant movement and its short-lived soviet—hence the ‘King of the Peasants.’ Betrayed and arrested in Shanghai in August 1929, he was shot at Longhua on 30 August 1929. The prison letters the author describes are preserved in the Collected Works of Peng Pai. Corroborated.

ch07.anchor: transferred to the detention house of the Longhua Garrison Command
ch07.note: The Longhua Garrison Command, in the southern outskirts of Shanghai, held the Kuomintang’s military prison and execution ground, where many Communists were shot—Peng Pai in 1929 and the ‘Five Martyrs,’ among them the writer Rou Shi, in February 1931. The site is today the Longhua Martyrs’ Cemetery. Corroborated.

ch08.anchor: Xiyan's cousin Wan Xixian died of injustice at just this time
ch08.note: The source carries its own endnote here, which reads: ‘Wan Xixian once served as a member of the second Special Committee of the Hunan–Jiangxi border region of the CCP. See Selected Works of Mao Zedong, vol. 1, “The Struggle in the Jinggang Mountains,” the section “Problems of Party Organization” (four-volume edition, p. 76).’ Wan Xixian (宛希先, d. 1930), a native of Huangmei in Hubei, a cousin of the author’s first husband Wan Xiyan and an early leader on the Jinggangshan, was wrongly killed in the over-extended ‘elimination of counter-revolutionaries’ around 1930 and later posthumously rehabilitated. Corroborated.

ch08.anchor: which was the program of action for the second
ch08.note: The ‘Li Lisan line’ was the ultra-‘Left’ policy of mid-1930, set out in the resolution the author here carries, which held that a nationwide revolutionary high tide was imminent and ordered armed uprisings and general strikes to seize power in the major cities. The resulting insurrections failed, and the line was corrected at the Third Plenum of the Sixth Central Committee in September 1930. Corroborated.

ch08.anchor: In her book *My Father Deng Xiaoping*, Maomao gives a detailed account
ch08.note: ‘Maomao’ is Deng Rong (邓榕), Deng Xiaoping’s daughter, whose memoir My Father Deng Xiaoping is a standard source. Passing through Hong Kong in late 1929, Deng went on to Guangxi to lead the Baise Uprising (December 1929) and the Longzhou Uprising (February 1930), which founded the Seventh and Eighth Red Armies. Corroborated.

ch08.anchor: Comrades Guan Xiangying and Ren Bishi, who had formerly worked with He Chang
ch08.note: Guan Xiangying (关向应, 1902–1946), a Manchu from Jin County in Liaoning and an early Communist Youth League leader, was secretary of the Party’s Military Commission when he was arrested in Shanghai in 1931. His identity stayed hidden and he was freed some months later—the rescue that opens the next chapter—and he later became a leading Red Army political commissar. Corroborated.

ch09.anchor: to serve as head of the rescue department of the Mutual Aid General Association
ch09.note: The chapter’s title in the source, 营救部长, names this post—‘head of the Rescue Department’ of the Mutual Aid General Association, to which the author is appointed here—rather than meaning ‘to rescue a minister.’ The Rescue Department had its own staff, as the author notes below.

ch09.anchor: was Tan Yankai, military governor and governor of Hunan Province
ch09.note: Tan Yankai (谭延闿, 1880–1930), a Hunan native and Qing metropolitan graduate, governed Hunan three times and became a leading figure of the Nationalist government, serving as the first president of its Executive Yuan. As the author notes, he signed the Wuhan government’s 17 April 1927 order expelling Chiang Kai-shek; the two were later reconciled. Corroborated.

ch09.anchor: Rumor among the common folk had it that the Qianlong Emperor was in fact a Han Chinese
ch09.note: The Chen family of Haining produced high officials for generations under the Qing. A durable folk legend—dramatized in fiction, notably Jin Yong’s The Book and the Sword—held that the Qianlong Emperor was secretly a Han Chinese, a son of this Chen family exchanged at birth for a Manchu girl. Historians reject it, and the author is right to call it untrue. Corroborated as legend only.

The “September Eighteenth” Incident is the Mukden Incident of 18 September 1931: officers of Japan’s Kwantung Army staged a railway explosion outside Shenyang (Mukden) as the pretext for seizing all of Manchuria. In China the event is named by its date; the “special extra-large issue” here answered it. Corroborated by standard reference works.

ch09.anchor: both judges of the International Settlement like the old gentleman
ch09.note: So the source; earlier in this chapter it seats Chen Qishou on the bench of the French Concession’s Mixed Court. The two statements stand side by side in the original and are left as written.

ch10.anchor: After Gu Shunzhang's defection, the work of the Central
ch10.note: Gu Shunzhang (顾顺章), head of the Party’s Central Special Branch and keeper of its deepest operational secrets, was captured in Wuhan and defected to the Kuomintang in April 1931. His betrayal exposed the Shanghai underground and forced a wholesale overhaul of it; the crisis around Xiang Zhongfa recounted here followed directly. Corroborated.

ch10.anchor: one turn in the electric chair
ch10.note: ‘Electric chair’ renders the source’s dianyi (电椅) literally, but in a Republican-era interrogation it means an electric-shock torture chair, not the American execution device: the prisoner is shocked until he breaks and confesses, and survives. The image is of torture under questioning, not electrocution.

ch10.anchor: the timely discovery and reporting of Xiang Zhongfa's defection
ch10.note: Xiang Zhongfa was arrested in the Shanghai French Concession on 22 June 1931 — a consequence of Gu Shunzhang’s defection that April — and shot about a day later, on 24 June 1931; the Party did not publicly confirm his betrayal until some time after his death. The account of the author’s own part in the warning was first made public in Deng Rong’s My Father Deng Xiaoping (1993). The arrest and execution are corroborated; the precise mechanism by which the Party first learned of the defection is debated among historians, several competing accounts existing, and is given here as the memoir tells it.

ch11.anchor: code name in the Awakening Society at Tianjin
ch11.note: ‘Wu Hao’ (伍豪) was Zhou Enlai’s alias. The Awakening Society, founded in Tianjin on 16 September 1919, gave its twenty members secret code names drawn by lot from the numbers 1 to 50; Zhou drew 5 (wu) and so became ‘Wu Hao’ (Deng Yingchao drew 1), and he later kept it as a pen name. The counter-notice’s trick turned on a second alias of his, ‘Zhou Shaoshan’. Corroborated.

These figures describe the Central Soviet at the close of 1931, after the third counter-campaign and the joining of the southern-Jiangxi and western-Fujian base areas; the base later grew far larger (about 84,000 square kilometres by 1933). The Provisional Central Government of the Chinese Soviet Republic was established at Ruijin at the First National Soviet Congress, 7–20 November 1931. Corroborated.

ch11.anchor: had jointly renounced the Communist Party
ch11.note: The ‘Wu Hao Notices’ were planted in the Shanghai press by the Kuomintang in February 1932 to fake Zhou Enlai’s defection; in fact Zhou had left Shanghai for the Jiangxi Soviet in early December 1931. The Party’s rebuttal, the ‘Zhou Shaoshan’ notice of 4 March 1932, is on record. During the Cultural Revolution the Gang of Four dug the forged notices out again to attack Zhou as a historical traitor. Corroborated.

ch11.anchor: then a lawyer at the French Concession's Municipal Police
ch11.note: The source carries one of its own two editorial notes here, appended to Li Yimang’s quoted account: ‘Chen always practised under his own shingle and was not a lawyer of the Municipal Police; Li Yimang’s recollection is mistaken. — Author’s note.’ The author reinforces the correction in her own text a few paragraphs on.

The source’s second editorial note falls here, on the quoted notice above: ‘The original was set in vertical columns and unpunctuated; the punctuation in the passage above was supplied by Comrade Li Yimang.’ The notice is thus given in the classical, unpointed legal style of the 1932 newspaper, repointed by its later editor.

‘Lord Zhou’ (Zhou Gong, 周公) is an honorific for Zhou Enlai. Literally it is the Duke of Zhou, the revered statesman of the early Zhou dynasty and a byword for the loyal, selfless minister; the memoir returns to the epithet in the title of Chapter 20, ‘An Audience with Zhou Enlai’ (面谒周公).

Zhuge Liang (181–234), chancellor of Shu Han in the Three Kingdoms period, is the proverbial master strategist of Chinese storytelling, and a “female Zhuge” is a woman of uncommon resource. Zhou Enlai caps the compliment with the storyteller’s set formula for Zhuge Liang’s cleverness: one knit of the brow, and a stratagem springs to mind.

ch12.anchor: that Zeng Guofan had paid to have built
ch12.note: The memoir credits the building of the Yu Mansion (俞楼, by Solitary Hill on West Lake) to Zeng Guofan’s funding, but scholarship does not bear this out: the pavilion was raised in 1878 by subscription among Yu Yue’s own students, with Peng Yulin (彭玉麟) meeting part of the cost and inscribing its name. Zeng Guofan, Yu Yue’s examiner and patron, had died in 1872, six years before the Yu Mansion existed. Rendered as the author wrote it; the discrepancy is noted here rather than silently corrected.

The name Dinghui (定慧) joins two Buddhist terms, ding (定, meditative concentration, Sanskrit samādhi) and hui (慧, wisdom, prajñā). It also echoes the dying wish of the author’s father that she ‘cultivate both blessing and wisdom’ (福慧双修) and puns on her childhood pet name Ding’er. Hupao (虎跑) Temple in Hangzhou is indeed also called Dinghui Temple, so tea taken there supplied both the pun and the occasion for the new name.

The Yuanyuan qu (圆圆曲) by Wu Weiye (styled Meicun, 1609–1672) laments the fall of the Ming through the Ming general Wu Sangui, who—in the poem’s telling—opened the passes to the Manchus in a rage over the seizure of his beloved, the courtesan Chen Yuanyuan. The quoted couplet, ‘Bitter grief that the whole army donned white mourning; in a wrathful surge that lifted his cap, all for a lovely woman,’ is its most famous line; ‘the whole army’ renders liu jun (六军), the classical term for the imperial host.

Both rock inscriptions are puns. Xiangxiang (象象) plays on 象 ‘elephant’ and 像 ‘to resemble’ (both read xiang): the rock resembles an elephant, holds a large and a small elephant, and—the party joked—suited scholars who ate like elephants. Shishi (师狮) reverses the syllables of 狮师 ‘to take the lion as one’s teacher,’ punning on 师 ‘teacher’ and 狮 ‘lion’; it was carved just after the January 1932 fighting at Shanghai, when the ‘sleeping lion’ of China was said to be waking.

ch13.note: ‘Mr. Zhongkai’ is Liao Zhongkai (廖仲恺, 1877–1925), the Nationalist leader who built the alliance with the Communists and the policy of support for peasants and workers, assassinated by right-wing agents in 1925. He Xiangning, who delivered this appeal, was his widow; her invocation of his unfinished ‘will’ and of Sun Yat-sen’s 1924 reorganization of the Party gave her plea its moral authority within the Kuomintang.

ch13.anchor: "Debate of Cao Gui" in the Zuo Commentary
ch13.note: The Cao Gui lun zhan (曹刿论战) is a celebrated passage in the Zuo Commentary (Duke Zhuang, tenth year): the Duke of Lu wins Cao Gui’s confidence to give battle by pledging to judge lawsuits great and small ‘according to their true circumstances.’ Lin Gengbai cited it to argue that clemency toward prisoners was itself the mark of just governance that made a cause worth fighting for.

The ‘Seven Gentlemen’ (七君子) were seven leaders of the National Salvation Association—Shen Junru, Zou Taofen, Li Gongpu, Sha Qianli, Shi Liang, Zhang Naiqi and Wang Zaoshi—arrested on 23 November 1936 on a charge of ‘endangering the Republic’ for pressing resistance to Japan, and released on 31 July 1937 after the war began. Corroborated.

ch13.anchor: Fifth Plenary Session of the Third National Congress
ch13.note: So the source (三届五次全国代表大会), an anomalous designation — a national congress has no numbered plenary sessions of this kind. From the November 1935 date, the meeting intended is evidently the Kuomintang’s Fifth National Congress, which opened in Nanjing on 12 November 1935. Rendered as the source has it.

ch14.anchor: In the winter of 1935, this Chairman Huang lost money
ch14.note: The memoir dates the Tongyi Company’s collapse to the winter of 1935 and its resumption to 1935–36; some later Shanghai banking histories place the failure in 1936. The essentials—a chairman surnamed Huang, bankruptcy under the weight of the creditors’ losses, and an unusual court-approved resumption of business—are attested, though the case is only lightly documented.

ch14.anchor: the drinker's heart was not in the cup
ch14.note: An allusion to Ouyang Xiu’s Record of the Old Toper’s Pavilion: ‘the old toper’s heart is not in the wine’ (醉翁之意不在酒)—that is, one’s true purpose lies elsewhere. The author’s real aim in the Tongyi affair was not banking but the standing and connections it opened for the Party’s united-front work.

That Qu Qiubai’s letters and Fang Zhimin’s prison writings were kept in the Tongyi Company’s vault and later taken out by A Ying and handed to the Central Propaganda Department is the author’s own testimony. Standard scholarship traces the surviving custody of Fang Zhimin’s prison manuscripts (among them Dear China) chiefly through Feng Xuefeng and Xie Danru; the Tongyi vault’s role in sheltering these particular papers is plausible but not independently established.

The source’s 民社党 is the (Chinese) Democratic Socialist Party — the name that Zhang Junmai’s National Socialist Party of China took only in 1946, applied by the memoir retrospectively to these mid-1930s events. A small constitutionalist party of intellectuals, it had no connection with the German National Socialists.

ch15.note: The memoir dates the founding of the All-Circles National Salvation Federation (全国各界救国联合会) to 31 May 1931, and places it before Song Qingling’s 1932 China League for the Protection of Civil Rights; but scholarship dates the Federation’s founding to 31 May 1936, five years later—the League for Civil Rights (founded winter 1932–33) in fact came first. The ‘Seven Gentlemen’ whose arrest this chapter goes on to recount were the Federation’s leaders, seized in November 1936, which accords with the 1936 date. Rendered as the author wrote it; the discrepancy is noted here rather than silently corrected.

Rao Jiaju (饶家驹) is the Chinese name of the French Jesuit Robert Jacquinot de Besange (1878–1946), the ‘One-Armed Father.’ In November 1937 he negotiated with the Japanese, French, and Chinese sides to establish the Nanshi (South City) Refugee Zone in Shanghai—the ‘Jacquinot Safe Zone’—which sheltered some three hundred thousand civilians and became a precedent for the neutral zones later written into the Fourth Geneva Convention of 1949. He lost his right arm not in the war but in a 1914 accident with fireworks at the Xujiahui (Zikawei) school where he taught; the memoir’s attribution to German shellfire in the First World War is the popular legend attached to the ‘One-Armed Father,’ and is contradicted by the record. The safe-zone work is well corroborated.

ch15.anchor: a three-day charity performance in aid of Suiyuan
ch15.note: The reissue here carries a photograph of the author and her sister-in-law—her husband’s sister—Chen Bingzhang, in the stage costume of the opera Selling Horses (贩马记), from this 1936 benefit. On it the author later inscribed a quatrain: ‘For the benefit to aid Suiyuan our cooperation was sincere; that year, sister and sister-in-law, we rejoiced with one heart. White-haired, we meet again and gladly talk of old times; children and grandchildren about our knees, we celebrate the revival.’ The photograph is given as a figure and its inscription in this note, so as not to break the narrative it interrupts in the source.

ch15.anchor: a newly written Peking opera, Liang Hongyu
ch15.note: Liang Hongyu (梁红玉, d. c. 1135), a woman general of the Southern Song and wife of the general Han Shizhong, is remembered for beating the war drum from the deck to rally the troops against the invading Jin army at the battle of Huangtiandang (1130). Staged to hearten resistance against Japan, her stand against a northern invader made a pointed parallel; Guo Moruo’s impromptu quatrain plays her name against that of the actress Jin Suqin who took the role.

ch16.note: These English names are provisional reconstructions of the source’s transliterations (孙特士·斐士 and 拿门·鲍纳), the two British principals of the Hong Kong-registered University Book Company under whose names the Daily Translation Herald was published to evade Japanese censorship. The original English names could not be verified; the forms given here are approximate.

The ‘three-thirds system’ (三三制) was the Communist Party’s united-front formula of the resistance years for apportioning places roughly equally among Communists, non-Party progressives, and centrist elements. Liu Shaowen’s point is that the ‘Tuesday Dining Club’—a standing weekly gathering of Shanghai intellectuals and notables of many backgrounds—anticipated that formula in the ‘white’ (Nationalist- and enemy-held) areas, and became a seedbed of the figures who later filled the eight legally recognized ‘democratic parties.’

Red Star Over China (西行漫记, literally ‘random notes on a journey to the west’), Edgar Snow’s 1937 account of the Communist base at Yan’an, is not to be confused with the ‘Sketches of the Westward Journey’ (西行漫画) named earlier in this chapter—a wholly separate album of Long March cartoons by Huang Zhen, later reissued as the Long March Album (长征画册). The two Chinese titles differ by a single character (记 ‘notes’ versus 画 ‘pictures’).

ch16.anchor: While the Xiongnu are not yet destroyed
ch16.note: The retort of the young Han general Huo Qubing (140–117 BC) when Emperor Wu offered to build him a mansion — a proverbial pledge to put the country before home and family, recorded in Sima Qian’s Records of the Grand Historian.

ch17.note: The China Defence League (保卫中国大同盟) was founded by Song Qingling in Hong Kong on 14 June 1938 to publicize China’s resistance abroad and channel international donations to the Communist-led Eighth Route and New Fourth Armies. The date and place are corroborated by the historical record.

Ho Chi Minh (胡志明, 1890–1969), later president of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam. Two details of the memoir’s account do not square with the record: he is not documented to have taken the name ‘Ho Chi Minh’ or held any ‘Chairman’ title until about 1940–45, and in 1939 he was based inland in South China (Guangxi and Yunnan) rather than at the Vietnamese port of Haiphong. The meeting and the hand-carved seal are the memoir’s own recollection and are otherwise uncorroborated. ‘Scholar in the Saddle’ renders 戎马书生 (rongma shusheng), a man of letters turned soldier.

The East River guerrillas — the Communist-led anti-Japanese force in the East River (Dongjiang) region of Guangdong, forerunner of the East River Column (东江纵队) — carried out the 1942 evacuation of prominent figures from Japanese-occupied Hong Kong recounted in Chapter 19.

“Hilaire Noulens” and his wife (their real names were Yakov Rudnik and Tatyana Moiseenko), Comintern liaison officers arrested in Shanghai in June 1931. Their case became an international cause célèbre, with a defense committee joined by Song Qingling and prominent Western intellectuals; sentenced to life imprisonment, they were released in 1937. Corroborated by standard accounts of the Comintern apparatus in Shanghai.

ch18.anchor: Chen Di’s nephew, General Chen Ce
ch18.note: Chen Ce (陈策, 1893–1949), the Kuomintang ‘one-legged admiral,’ better known in English as Chan Chak. On 25 December 1941, the day Hong Kong surrendered, he led some sixty men out of the colony by motor torpedo boat to Mirs Bay and then overland to the mainland — a celebrated escape. The lost leg and the escape are both corroborated.

The Zhongshan (中山舰, formerly the Yongfeng) was a gunboat famous in Republican history, notably for the 1926 ‘Zhongshan Warship Incident.’ That a man named Chen Di (陈涤) once captained her is not found in the available scholarship and is given here on the memoir’s authority alone.

ch18.anchor: invite him to work on the peace-maintenance committee
ch18.note: A ‘peace-maintenance committee’ (维持会) was a collaborationist body of local notables that the Japanese set up to run an occupied town until a regular puppet administration could be installed. To refuse to head or serve on one, as Chen Di did, was an act of open defiance.

ch19.note: Yang Huimin (杨惠敏, c. 1915–1992), a young Girl Guide who on the night of 28 October 1937 crossed Suzhou Creek to deliver a national flag to Colonel Xie Jinyuan and the defenders of the Sihang Warehouse — the ‘Eight Hundred Heroes,’ a garrison of some four hundred publicized as eight hundred — during the Battle of Shanghai. The episode is corroborated and made her a national celebrity.

ch19.anchor: a rescue on a grand scale
ch19.note: This is the operation later known as the ‘Great Rescue’ (胜利大营救). Between January and November 1942 the Communist Party, through the Guangdong guerrillas (forerunner of the East River Column), evacuated more than eight hundred cultural figures and democratic personages, along with their relatives and international friends, from Japanese-occupied Hong Kong. Mao Dun, himself among the rescued, called it the greatest work of rescue since the War of Resistance began. The scale and the roster of those saved are corroborated.

Lin Gengbai (林庚白, 1896–1941), a poet of the Southern Society. On 19 December 1941 he was shot dead by Japanese soldiers near the observatory in Kowloon and his wife Lin Beili was wounded, as the memoir recounts; he was forty-five. The date, the circumstances, and his age are corroborated. He appears in passing in earlier chapters; the note is placed here, where his death is the subject.

Qu Yingguang (屈映光, style name Wenliu, 1883–1973), a native of Linhai in Zhejiang who briefly served as the province’s military governor in 1916 and was appointed a vice-chairman of the Nationalist government’s Relief Commission in 1938. The particulars are corroborated.

ch20.anchor: the Great Yu, who bowed when he heard good counsel
ch20.note: An allusion to Mencius (‘Gongsun Chou I’): ‘When Yu heard a good word, he bowed.’ The sage-king Yu the Great is the model of a leader humble enough to bow in thanks for good advice; Zhou Enlai invokes him to urge an open, self-correcting temper.

ch20.anchor: drop the watermelon to pick up sesame seeds
ch20.note: A play on the common saying ‘to pick up the sesame seed and drop the watermelon’ (捡了芝麻，丢了西瓜) — to grasp at the trivial and let the important slip. Zhou puns on the actual watermelon the children are eating, warning the author not to give up a vital post over a personal grievance.

ch20.anchor: fourteen anti-Japanese base areas behind enemy lines
ch20.note: Zhou’s figure as the author reports it. The canonical count of Communist-led anti-Japanese base areas is the ‘nineteen Liberated Areas’ cited at the Party’s Seventh Congress in 1945; the number grew through the war, and ‘fourteen’ is not a standard, datable figure for 1942. Rendered as spoken, and not to be read as an established statistic.

In January 1941 Kuomintang forces ambushed the headquarters column of the Communist-led New Fourth Army as it moved through southern Anhui, destroying most of it; commander Ye Ting was taken prisoner (see the note on him in the next chapter) and deputy commander Xiang Ying was killed. The CCP counts this the peak of the Kuomintang’s “second anti-Communist high tide.” Corroborated by standard histories.

ch21.anchor: Guan Yunchang taking his leave of Cao Cao, sealing up the gold and hanging up his seal
ch21.note: An allusion to Romance of the Three Kingdoms: when Guan Yu (Guan Yunchang) left Cao Cao to rejoin his sworn lord Liu Bei, he sealed up untouched all the gold Cao had lavished on him and hung up his seal of office — a byword for incorruptible integrity in departure.

The Loyal and Patriotic National Salvation Army (忠义救国军) was a genuine Dai Li–controlled irregular force. Its Hengyang-region commander is named here as ‘Zhou Kuilong’ (周夔龙), the ‘One-Eyed Dragon,’ a first-class Whampoa graduate; scholarship records the army’s commander from 1940 as Zhou Weilong (周伟龙), and neither the ‘One-Eyed Dragon’ nickname nor the first-class-Whampoa detail is corroborated. The name is very likely a slip for Zhou Weilong. That Dai Li himself was of the sixth Whampoa class and left without graduating, as the author notes, is corroborated.

ch21.anchor: carried the wounded Chiang Kai-shek down a mountain on his back
ch21.note: Ye Ting’s capture after the Southern Anhui Incident of January 1941 and his years of Nationalist imprisonment are well documented (he was released in March 1946 and died in an air crash that April). The particular story that he once carried a wounded Chiang Kai-shek down a mountain on his back is not found in the historical record, and is given here on the memoir’s authority alone.

ch21.anchor: Shen Baoxu weeping at the Qin court
ch21.note: An allusion to the Zuo Commentary: when Chu was overrun, its envoy Shen Baoxu stood weeping at the court of Qin for seven days and nights until Qin sent troops to save it — a figure for pleading with utter, self-abasing persistence to rescue another.

ch21.anchor: the three armies may be robbed of their commander, but a common man cannot be robbed of his will
ch21.note: The closing line is from the Analects (IX.26): ‘The three armies may be robbed of their commander, but a common man cannot be robbed of his will.’ The author sets Confucius’s words as the coda to her prison defense, pledging that her resolve could not be broken.

ch39.note: This afterword is the author’s own valedictory verse — ten couplets in the classical four-character measure — composed at Hangzhou in the winter of 2002, in her ninety-sixth year. She sums up a life in the clandestine service through the modest self-image of a “diligent old soldier” whose task was only to sweep away the dust (专司打扫，内外微尘), her recurring figure for underground and secretarial work.

“The sweet-pear tree’s kindly grace” (甘棠德泽) alludes to the Classic of Poetry (“Shao Nan: Gan Tang”): cherishing the just rule of the Lord of Shao, the people would not cut down the sweet-pear tree under which he had rested and given judgment. It stands for benevolent rule gratefully remembered.

ch39.anchor: an old steed at the stall
ch39.note: “An old steed at the stall” echoes Cao Cao’s Though the Tortoise Lives Long (龟虽寿): “The aged steed in its stall still sets its heart on a thousand li; the hero in his twilight years, his fighting spirit undimmed.” Past ninety, the author claims that undiminished aspiration for herself.

ch40.note: Her detention in June 1955 came as part of the case against Pan Hannian (潘汉年), the senior intelligence official under whom she had worked in Shanghai and Hong Kong; Pan was arrested in April 1955, and suspicion of the wartime underground’s contacts swept up many who had served in it. Across two spells at Qincheng she lost some seventeen years of freedom; she was declared innocent and rehabilitated in 1980, and Pan himself was posthumously cleared in 1982. The prisoner numbers the chronology records — 1067 here, 513 at Qincheng in 1959 — are the source’s own.

ch40.anchor: find and confirm the site of the First Congress
ch40.note: The site of the Chinese Communist Party’s First Congress of July 1921, a shikumen house on today’s Xingye Road in Shanghai, was located and authenticated in 1950–1952. Bao Huiseng (包惠僧), himself a delegate to the 1921 congress, was among those consulted to confirm the address, and the house opened as a memorial site in 1952. The chronology records the author’s part in retrieving the Tongyi materials and helping identify it.

“Honorable retirement” renders lixiu (离休), a status distinct from ordinary retirement (退休) reserved for veteran cadres who had joined the revolution before 1949; it carried fuller pay and standing in recognition of that service.

ch41.note: The appendix gives Liu Shaowen’s original name as Liu Zizhang (刘自章); standard reference works instead attest Liu Guozhang (刘国章), the two differing only in the middle character, so one is likely a slip. The memoir’s form is kept here. His dates (1905–1987), his Henan origin, and his 1955 rank of lieutenant general are corroborated.

Nikolai Ostrovsky’s Soviet novel How the Steel Was Tempered, long hugely influential in China. The account here is corroborated: in April 1938 Liu Shaowen handed the book to Mei Yi as a task assigned by the Party organization, and Mei Yi translated it from Alec Brown’s 1937 English version; his was the first Chinese translation, published in 1942 by the New Knowledge Bookstore.

The closing figure, an “underground Great Wall” (地下长城), is the title of the ci poem to the tune “The Immortal by the River” that the author set at the head of Part Two, on the Party’s clandestine front. This appendix — a tribute to the intelligence veteran Liu Shaowen — was excerpted from a People’s Daily article of 10 June 1996 by Luo Qingchang and Chai Chengwen, both long-serving figures of the Party’s intelligence establishment.

ch42.note: This tribute is by the author’s granddaughter Chen Hongxin (陈弘欣), who signs it from Sydney, Australia, in August 2003 — hence the “southern hemisphere.” It is one of two family afterwords the book prints, the other being the editors’ postscript by the author’s two daughters.

On leaving Qincheng in 1975 the author was barred, under the rule of the day — that she might not stay in the capital or go to a big city or the frontier — and was taken to Daye in Hubei, where her daughter’s family was posted with a geological survey team. It was there, the granddaughter recalls, that she at once took up the petitions that grew into this memoir.

ch42.anchor: Professor Dena Gutman of Stanford University
ch42.note: The closing quotation is the granddaughter’s. The authority she cites — a “Professor Dena Gutman” of Stanford University and a book rendered A New Culture, a New Stage (Stanford University Press, 1997) — could not be traced in any library catalog or scholarly record, and both the name and the title appear garbled; no such author or work has been located. The passage is given as she quotes it, with this caveat.

ch43.note: The postscript is by the author’s two daughters, Chen Yunzhong and Chen Dazhong (their signatures close it). It traces the book’s making: dictated onto cassette tapes after she settled in Hangzhou in 1993 and transcribed by work-study students, edited from 1996 by Ye Bingnan of the Zhejiang CPPCC, a first draft finished in 2000, a second by the cousin Qian Lin, and background notes for younger readers added in this third draft.

ch43.anchor: this September Uncle Mei suddenly left us
ch43.note: Mei Yi (梅益, 1913–2003), the translator and broadcasting official who had backed the memoir and undertaken to write its preface, died on 13 September 2003; this postscript is dated that December. His death is corroborated.

ch43.anchor: The Monument to the Nameless Heroes standing in Tiananmen Square
ch43.note: The monument that stands in Tiananmen Square is in fact the Monument to the People’s Heroes (人民英雄纪念碑); there is no separate “nameless heroes” monument there. A dedicated Monument to the Nameless Heroes, for the Party’s hidden-front martyrs, was later raised at Xishan in western Beijing and unveiled in December 2013, a decade after this postscript was written.
